objectives.label: Equal ordered pairs
objectives.description: Find unknown values by equating the corresponding components of equal ordered pairs, and plot ordered pairs.

objectives.label: Finding cartesian products
objectives.description: Find the cartesian product X×Y of two finite sets, including X², and calculate the number of its elements n(X×Y).

objectives.label: Arrow and cartesian diagrams
objectives.description: Represent the cartesian product of finite sets by an arrow diagram and a cartesian diagram.

objectives.label: Graphing infinite cartesian products
objectives.description: Represent products of infinite sets such as N×N, Z×Z, Q×Q and R×R on a perpendicular graphical net, identify ordered pairs of points, and locate points by quadrant or axis.

entries.text: You have previously studied relation between two variables x, y

A.why: Assumed prior knowledge about relations between two variables, not taught here.

B.why: Prior knowledge about relations assumed by the lesson.

entries.text: In each ordered pair (a, b), a is called the first projection and b is called the second projection. $(a,b)$

A.why: Names the components of an ordered pair, used when equating corresponding components.

B.why: Introduces the terms first and second projection at the start of the lesson.

entries.text: Each ordered pair is represented by one and only one point in the coordinate plane.

A.why: Each ordered pair is one point in the plane, which is the plotting of ordered pairs.

B.why: Each ordered pair is one point, underlying plotting pairs.

entries.text: If a ≠ b then (a, b) ≠ (b, a). The page asks 'Why?' with no printed answer. $a\neq b \Rightarrow (a,b)\neq(b,a)$

A.why: Unequal order means unequal pairs, like (3,5) versus (5,3) in the equality activity.

B.why: Order matters, so unequal pairs, tied to equality of ordered pairs.

entries.text: The ordered pair (a, b) is not equal to the set {a, b}. $(a,b)\neq\{a,b\}$

A.why: Distinguishes an ordered pair from a set, part of the ordered-pair equality ideas.

B.why: General remark on ordered pairs versus sets, introducing the lesson.

entries.text: Table for X×Y: rows first projection a, b; columns second projection -1, 0, 3 ×, -1, 0, 3 / a, (a, -1), (a, 0), (a, 3) / b, (b, -1), (b, 0), (b, 3)

A.why: Table listing the elements of X×Y.

B.why: Table listing the pairs of X×Y.

entries.text: Table for Y×X: rows first projection -1, 0, 3; columns second projection a, b ×, a, b / -1, (-1, a), (-1, b) / 0, (0, a), (0, b) / 3, (3, a), (3,b)

A.why: Table listing the elements of Y×X, for comparison with X×Y.

B.why: Table listing the pairs of Y×X.

entries.text: X×Y ≠ Y×X where X ≠ Y. $X\times Y\neq Y\times X$

A.why: States X×Y ≠ Y×X, following the worked example of X×Y and Y×X.

B.why: X×Y differs from Y×X, from the worked example comparison.

entries.text: The number of elements of X×Y equals that of Y×X, which equals n(X) times n(Y). $n(X\times Y)=n(Y\times X)=n(X)\times n(Y)$

A.why: Gives n(X×Y) = n(X)×n(Y), the counting of elements.

B.why: Number of elements of X×Y equals n(X)×n(Y).

entries.text: n denotes the number of set elements.

A.why: Notation n for number of elements, used in counting n(X×Y).

B.why: Notation n for counting elements of the product.

entries.text: If (k, m) ∈ X×Y then k ∈ X and m ∈ Y. $(k,m)\in X\times Y\Rightarrow k\in X,\ m\in Y$

A.why: Says what membership in X×Y means for the components.

B.why: Says what membership in X×Y means for the components.

entries.text: If X is a non-empty set then X×X = {(a, b) : a, b ∈ X}. $X\times X=\{(a,b):a,b\in X\}$

A.why: Defines X×X, part of finding cartesian products.

B.why: Defines X×X as a set of pairs.

entries.text: X×X is written X² and read "X two". $X\times X=X^2$

A.why: Notation X² for X×X.

B.why: Notation X² for X×X belongs to finding products.

entries.text: Venn diagram: X is a separate circle containing 1; Z is a circle containing 5, 6 and 2; Y is an overlapping oval containing 2 and 3, overlapping Z at 2. Labels Z, X, Y on the circles.

A.why: Venn diagram of sets X, Y, Z used for finding products of finite sets.

B.why: Venn diagram of sets not tied to a particular objective.

entries.text: Arrow diagram X × Y: set X oval with elements 1, 2; set Y oval with elements 3, 4, 5; arrows from 1 to 3, 4, 5 and from 2 to 3, 4, 5. Arrows read from the figure; verify.

A.why: Arrow diagram of X×Y for the worked example.

B.why: Arrow diagram of X×Y in the worked example.

entries.text: Cartesian graph net X × Y: horizontal axis X with 1, 2; vertical axis Y with 3, 4, 5; intersection points labelled (1,3), (2,3), (1,4), (2,4), (1,5), (2,5). Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Cartesian diagram of X×Y for the same example.

B.why: Cartesian diagram of X×Y in the worked example.

entries.text: Arrow Diagram: three points 3 (top), 4 (bottom right), 8 (bottom left); loops at 3 and 4 (and 8); arrows between each pair of points in both directions. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Arrow diagram of X×X for X={3,4,8}.

B.why: Arrow diagram of X×X for X={3,4,8}.

entries.text: If n(X) = 3, then n(X × X) = 3 × 3 = 9. $n(X)=3\Rightarrow n(X\times X)=3\times3=9$

A.why: Counts the elements of X×X when n(X)=3.

B.why: Counts the elements of X×X from n(X).

entries.text: Step 2: Represent the natural numbers N on each of the horizontal and vertical straight lines, starting with the origin point O which represents the number zero.

A.why: Step in drawing the graphical net of N×N.

B.why: Step of marking natural numbers on the axes of the net.

entries.text: Step 3: Draw vertical and horizontal straight lines from the points representing the natural numbers; the points of intersection of these lines are represented by the perpendicular graphical net of the cartesian product N × N.

A.why: Step giving the net points of N×N.

B.why: Step of drawing the N×N perpendicular graphical net.

entries.text: Graphical net for N×N: x'x horizontal axis and y'y vertical axis meeting at origin O (0); horizontal marks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; vertical marks 1, 2, 3, 4. Point A at (3, 2), point B at (0, 4) on the y-axis, point C on the x-axis at 5 (read from the figure; verify).

A.why: Graphical net for N×N with points A, B, C.

B.why: N×N graphical net with points A, B, C.

entries.text: Notice that: each point of this net represents one of the ordered pairs in the cartesian product of N × N.

A.why: Each net point represents a pair of N×N.

B.why: Each point of the N×N net represents a pair of N×N.

entries.text: Each point of the net represents one of the pairs in the cartesian product Z × Z.

A.why: Each net point represents a pair of Z×Z.

B.why: Each point of the Z×Z net represents a pair of the product.

entries.text: This net is known as the coordinate plane of Z × Z.

A.why: Names the net the coordinate plane of Z×Z.

B.why: Names the net as the coordinate plane of Z×Z.

entries.text: Coordinate plane of Z×Z with axes x'x and y'y, origin O, integer marks -4 to 4 on x-axis and -4 to 4 on y-axis. Points: A at about (3, 3), B at about (4, -2), C at about (-3, 1), D at about (-3, -4) (read from figure; verify).

A.why: Coordinate plane of Z×Z with labelled points to identify.

B.why: Z×Z net with points A to D whose pairs are to be identified.

entries.text: The horizontal straight line xx' is called the x-axis.

A.why: Names the x-axis of the plane.

B.why: Names the x-axis of the graphical net.

entries.text: The vertical straight line yy' is called the y-axis.

A.why: Names the y-axis of the plane.

B.why: Names the y-axis of the graphical net.

entries.text: Coordinate plane with x-axis (x' to x) and y-axis (y to y'), origin O, tick marks -4 to 4. First quadrant (upper right): x>0, y>0. Second quadrant (upper left): x<0, y>0. Third quadrant (lower left): x<0, y<0. Fourth quadrant (lower right): x>0, y<0.

A.why: Shows the four quadrants of the plane.

B.why: Shows the quadrants of the coordinate plane, used to locate points by quadrant.

entries.text: Square grid with x-axis and y-axis, origin O, ticks -4 to 4. Plotted points: A (3, 3), D (-4, 3), C (-4, -2), B (3, -2), E (0, -3) on y-axis, F (2, 0) on x-axis.

A.why: Points in quadrants and on the axes of the plane.

B.why: Plotted points with read-off coordinates illustrate plotting ordered pairs in the plane.

objectives.label: Write relations as ordered pairs
objectives.description: Write a relation from a set X to a set Y as a set of ordered pairs, using the rule connecting a and b (e.g. b = 2a + 4, or 'a is a digit of b').

objectives.label: Represent relations by diagrams
objectives.description: Represent a relation by an arrow diagram and by a cartesian diagram.

objectives.label: Relations as subsets of X × Y
objectives.description: Determine whether a relation is a subset of the cartesian product X × Y, decide which ordered pairs satisfy the stated relation, and identify a relation on a set X as R ⊂ X × X.

entries.text: Picture of people holding up books, labelled 'Reading for all' (decorative-ish illustration).

A.why: Decorative 'Reading for all' picture introducing the lesson.

B.why: Decorative illustration introducing the lesson.

entries.text: Arrow diagram from X={a,b,c,d,e} to Y={Science, art, culture, history}. Arrows: a→Science, a→culture, b→history, c→culture(?), e→history; d has no arrow. Y lists 'art' where text says literature.

A.why: Arrow diagram of the relation from X to Y.

B.why: Arrow diagram showing the relation from X to Y.

entries.text: The set of ordered pairs {(a, Science), (a, Culture), (b, Histrory), (c, Literature), (e, History)} expresses the relation from X to Y and is called the relation R.

A.why: Expresses the relation as a set of ordered pairs.

B.why: Expresses the relation as a set of ordered pairs.

entries.text: Arrow diagram from X to Y: X = {-1, 1, 2}, Y = {2, 4, 6, 8}; arrows -1→2, 1→6, 2→8.

A.why: Arrow diagram of the relation from X to Y.

B.why: Arrow diagram of the relation from X to Y.

entries.text: Graph diagram with X axis marks -1, 1, 2 and Y axis marks 2, 4, 6, 8; points plotted at (-1, 2), (1, 6), (2, 8).

A.why: Graph (cartesian) diagram showing the relation's ordered pairs.

B.why: Graph (cartesian) diagram of the relation from X to Y.

entries.text: A relation from X to Y, where X and Y are two non-empty sets, connects some or all elements of X with some or all elements of Y.

A.why: States that a relation connects elements of X with elements of Y, leading to R as a subset of X × Y.

B.why: States what a relation from X to Y is, connecting some or all elements, leading to the subset of X × Y idea.

entries.text: X × Y is the set of ordered pairs where the first projection in each pair belongs to X and the second projection belongs to Y. $X\times Y$

A.why: Defines X × Y, the product of which a relation is a subset.

B.why: Defines X × Y, the cartesian product that a relation is a subset of.

entries.text: Arrow diagram of R on X: number line with arcs linking -2↔2, -1↔1 and a loop at 0; also an oval with X = {-2,-1,0,1,2} showing a loop on 0 and double arrows between -1 and 1, -2 and 2.

A.why: Arrow diagram of a relation on X.

B.why: Arrow diagram of relation R on X.

entries.text: Cartesian diagram with both axes marked -2 to 2; points plotted at (-2, 2), (-1, 1), (0, 0), (1, -1), (2, -2).

A.why: Cartesian diagram of the relation on X.

B.why: Cartesian diagram plotting the ordered pairs of the relation on X.

objectives.label: Identify functions
objectives.description: Decide whether a relation, given as arrow diagram, cartesian diagram or ordered pairs, is a function by checking that each element of X has only one image.

objectives.label: Symbolic representation of functions
objectives.description: Write a function using the symbols f : X \to Y, f(x) = y and as a set of ordered pairs, and represent it by an arrow diagram and a cartesian diagram.

objectives.label: Domain, codomain and range
objectives.description: Determine the domain, codomain and range of a function, noting the range is a subset of the codomain.

entries.text: Three arrow diagrams (1), (2), (3) from set X = {2, 3, 5, 7} to set Y = {1, 4, 6, 8, 9}, with arrows between elements. Individual arrows cannot be read reliably from the image; verify against the page.

A.why: Arrow diagrams from X to Y used to decide which relations are functions.

B.why: Arrow diagrams from X to Y in the opening activity on which relations are functions.

entries.text: A function is denoted by one of the symbols f, m, Q, ...; the function f from the set X to the set Y is written $f : X \to Y$ and read "f is a function from X to Y". $f : X \to Y$

A.why: Gives the symbol f : X → Y for writing a function.

B.why: Gives the symbol f : X → Y for writing a function.

entries.text: If f is a function from X to itself, f is called a function on X.

A.why: Naming a function on X is part of the notation for functions f : X → X.

B.why: Naming convention for a function on X, part of function notation.

entries.text: Arrow diagram (printed 'Arrow digaram') of f on X: elements 4, 5, 6, 3. Arrows: 3→3 (loop), 4→5, 5→4, 6→5.

A.why: Arrow diagram representing the function f given in the worked example.

B.why: Arrow diagram representing the function f from the worked example.

entries.text: Cartesian diagram with x-axis X marked 3, 4, 5, 6 and y-axis X marked 3, 4, 5, 6; dots at (3,3), (4,5), (5,4), (6,5).

A.why: Cartesian diagram representing the same function f.

B.why: Cartesian diagram representing the function f from the worked example.

entries.text: Arrow diagram (1) on X with elements 1, 2, 3, 4, with arrows among them.

A.why: Arrow diagram in the exercise asking which represent a function on X.

B.why: Arrow diagram in the exercise on which represent a function on X.

entries.text: Arrow diagram (2) on X with elements 1, 2, 3, 4, with arrows among them.

A.why: Arrow diagram in the exercise asking which represent a function on X.

B.why: Arrow diagram in the exercise on which represent a function on X.

entries.text: Arrow diagram (3) on X with elements 1, 2, 3, 4, with arrows among them.

A.why: Arrow diagram in the exercise asking which represent a function on X.

B.why: Arrow diagram in the exercise on which represent a function on X.

entries.text: Cartesian diagram (1), axes X with values 1 to 5; dots at (3,5), (4,4), (2,3), (1,2), (3,2).

A.why: Cartesian diagram in the exercise on whether it is a function (3 has two images).

B.why: Cartesian diagram in the exercise on which diagrams are functions from X to X.

entries.text: Cartesian diagram (2), axes X with values 1 to 5; dots at (1,3), (2,3), (3,3), (4,3), (5,3).

A.why: Cartesian diagram in the exercise on whether it is a function.

B.why: Cartesian diagram in the exercise on which diagrams are functions from X to X.

entries.text: Cartesian diagram (3), axes X with values 1 to 5; dots at (1,1), (2,2), (4,4), (5,5).

A.why: Cartesian diagram in the exercise on whether it is a function (element 3 has no image).

B.why: Cartesian diagram in the exercise on which diagrams are functions from X to X.

entries.text: The set X is called the domain of the function f.

A.why: Defines the domain of a function.

B.why: Defines the domain.

entries.text: The set Y is called the codomain of the function f.

A.why: Defines the codomain of a function.

B.why: Defines the codomain.

A.why: Arrow diagram for the worked example finding domain, codomain and range.

B.why: Arrow diagram of the domain/codomain/range worked example.

entries.text: The range is a subset of the codomain of the function.

A.why: States the range is a subset of the codomain.

B.why: States the range is a subset of the codomain.

entries.text: Arrow diagram from X to Y. X = {2, 3, 4}; Y = {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. Arrows: 2→4, 3→6, 4→8.

A.why: Arrow diagram used to find domain, codomain and range.

B.why: Arrow diagram with Y larger than the images shows codomain versus range.

objectives.label: Identify polynomials and degree
objectives.description: Identify polynomial functions and state their degree from the function rule.

objectives.label: Evaluate function values
objectives.description: Calculate the image of a given value (including surds) under a polynomial function.

objectives.label: Graph linear and constant functions
objectives.description: Represent a linear function or constant function graphically by finding ordered pairs and drawing the straight line.

objectives.label: Graph quadratic functions
objectives.description: Represent a quadratic function graphically and state its vertex, axis of symmetry and maximum or minimum value.

entries.text: The degree of the polynomial is the highest power of the variable in the function rule.

A.why: Degree is the highest power of the variable in the rule.

B.why: States that the degree is the highest power of the variable in the rule.

entries.text: The function f: R → R where f(x) = ax + b, a, b ∈ R, a ≠ 0 is called a linear function or a function of the first degree. $f(x)=ax+b,\ a,b\in\mathbb{R},\ a\neq 0$

A.why: Linear function definition introduces the functions graphed next.

B.why: Defines a linear function as a first-degree polynomial, identified from its rule.

A.why: Ordered pairs for graphing f(x)=2x-3.

B.why: Ordered pairs for graphing f(x)=2x-3.

entries.text: Square-net coordinate plane with X'X and Y'Y axes; a straight line with arrows at both ends drawn through points (0,-3), (1,-1), (2,1), passing the x-axis between 1 and 2 (at 1.5); marked points in blue.

A.why: Straight-line graph of f(x)=2x-3.

B.why: Straight-line graph of f(x)=2x-3 from its ordered pairs.

entries.text: It is enough to find two ordered pairs belonging to the function; it is preferred to find a third ordered pair to check the graph.

A.why: Says how many ordered pairs are needed to draw the line.

B.why: Says two ordered pairs suffice to draw the line, with a third as a check.

entries.text: If f: R → R, f(x) = ax, where a ≠ 0, then it is represented graphically by a straight line passing through the origin (0, 0). $f(x)=ax,\ a\neq 0$

A.why: Graph of f(x)=ax is a line through the origin.

B.why: States that f(x)=ax graphs as a straight line through the origin.

entries.text: Values of the constant function f(x)=3 for x = -1, 1, 2 x, -1, 1, 2 / y = f(x), 3, 3, 3

A.why: Ordered pairs for the constant function f(x)=3.

B.why: Ordered pairs for graphing the constant function f(x)=3.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with axes x'x and y'y, x-axis marks -2, -1, 1, 2, y-axis mark 3. A horizontal line with arrows at both ends passes through y = 3, with three dots at about x = -1, 1 and 2, showing the graph of y = 3.

A.why: Horizontal line graph of the constant function y=3.

B.why: Graph of the constant function y=3 as a horizontal line.

entries.text: The function f: R → R where f(x) = ax² + bx + c, a, b, c real numbers, a ≠ 0, is called a quadratic function and it is a function of second degree. $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c,\ a\neq 0$

A.why: Defines the quadratic function that is then graphed.

B.why: Defines a quadratic function as a second-degree polynomial, identified by its rule and degree.

entries.text: Table of x values and y = f(x) for f(x)=x² x, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3 / y = f(x), 9, 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, 9

A.why: Values for graphing f(x)=x².

B.why: Values table used to plot f(x)=x².

entries.text: Cartesian plane with x'x and y'y axes, y marked 1 to 10, x marked -4 to 4. A blue parabola with vertex at origin (0,0), opening upwards, with dots at (-3,9), (-2,4), (-1,1), (0,0), (1,1), (2,4), (3,9).

A.why: Parabola of f(x)=x² with vertex at origin.

B.why: Graph of the parabola f(x)=x² with its vertex at the origin.

entries.text: The curve of the function f is symmetrical about the y-axis and the equation of the symmetrical axis is x = 0. $x=0$

A.why: Axis of symmetry of the curve is x=0.

B.why: Gives the axis of symmetry of the graph of x².

entries.text: The vertex of the curve is (0, 0), and the minimum value of the function = 0. $(0,0)$

A.why: States the vertex and minimum value of the curve.

B.why: Gives the vertex and minimum value for f(x)=x².

entries.text: The curve opens upwards when the coefficient of x² is positive (a > 0); the function then has a minimum value equal to f(-b/2a). $f\left(\frac{-b}{2a}\right)$

A.why: Opens upward with a minimum value when a>0.

B.why: States that a>0 gives a minimum value f(-b/2a).

entries.text: The curve opens downward when the coefficient of x² is negative (a < 0); the function then has a maximum value equal to f(-b/2a). $f\left(\frac{-b}{2a}\right)$

A.why: Opens downward with a maximum value when a<0.

B.why: States that a<0 gives a maximum value f(-b/2a).

entries.text: The curve is symmetric about the vertical line through the vertex, with equation X = -b/2a; this line is called the axis of symmetry of the function. $x=\frac{-b}{2a}$

A.why: Axis of symmetry is x=-b/2a.

B.why: States the axis of symmetry x=-b/2a of a quadratic curve.

A.why: Values for graphing f(x)=-x².

B.why: Values table used to plot the quadratic f(x)=-x².

entries.text: Graph on squared grid with axes x'x and y'y, x marked from -4 to 4 and y marked 1 to 9 downward (negative side). Downward-opening parabola with vertex at the origin (0,0), passing through points marked (±1,-1), (±2,-4), (±3,-9).

A.why: Downward parabola of f(x)=-x² with maximum at the vertex.

B.why: Graph of the downward parabola y=-x² with vertex at the origin.
